is async/await safe? is there some principled way to decide how far back of browsers we want to support?
02:15 Copilot Chat copilot/gemini-2.5-pro thought for 17s

That's an excellent and important question. Here's a breakdown of how to think about this:

Is async/await safe?

For the file we've been looking at, , the answer is a clear yes, it is safe. Here's why:

  • Server-Side Code: runs on your server using Node.js, not in a user's web browser. This means you don't have to worry about compatibility with older browsers like Internet Explorer.
  • Node.js Support: async/await has been fully supported in Node.js since version 8.0.0, which was released in May 2017. Any modern hosting environment or local development setup will be running a much newer version of Node.js, making async/await a standard and safe feature to use.

For client-side JavaScript (the code that runs in the browser), you would need to consider browser support, which leads to your next question.

How to decide on browser support?

Deciding which browsers to support is a strategic decision that balances reaching the widest audience with the cost and complexity of supporting older technology. Here are some principled ways to make that decision:

  1. Use Analytics Data (Most Important): The most data-driven approach is to look at your website's analytics (e.g., Google Analytics, Plausible, Fathom). Check the "Browser & OS" reports to see what browsers your actual users are using. If less than 1-2% of your audience is using an old browser, it's often acceptable to stop supporting it.
  1. Check Feature Support: Use a website like caniuse.com. You can search for a specific JavaScript or CSS feature (like async/await) and see a detailed chart of which browser versions support it. This helps you understand the impact of using a new feature.
  1. Follow Industry Standards: A common policy is to support the last two major versions of all major browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge). This is a good default because it covers the vast majority of users who have auto-updating browsers.
  1. Use Transpilers and Polyfills: You don't have to choose between modern code and older browser support. Tools like Babel can "transpile" your modern JavaScript (with async/await) into an older version (like ES5) that runs on nearly every browser. This is the standard practice for most modern web development, allowing you to write clean, modern code without sacrificing compatibility. Your project already has a , which suggests a build process is in place where a tool like Babel could be integrated.

In summary, for the server-side code, you can and should use modern features like async/await. For the client-side, the best practice is to write modern code and use a build tool like Babel to ensure it works for the browsers you need to support.

not all the timestamps are recent...

You are absolutely right to point that out, and my apologies for overlooking that detail. You've caught the reason why some timestamps are old, and it's actually a feature, not a bug.

The culprit is the gulp-changed plugin, which is used in the compress_js task:

// ...
.pipe(changed(LIBJS, { extension: '.min.js' }))
// ...

This is an optimization. The changed plugin checks if the source file (e.g., ) has been modified since its corresponding output file () was last created.

  • If the source file has not changed, gulp-changed stops it from going through the rest of the process (terser, rename, etc.). This saves time by not re-compressing files that are already up-to-date.
  • If the source file is newer, it gets passed along to be minified and rewritten, which updates its timestamp.

So, the old timestamps you're seeing are on files that haven't been edited recently. This is the expected and correct behavior of your build script. It's a sign that the optimization is working.

ok, that works. next question: why do we need these new suppressBrush and suppressZoom booleans?
23:19 Codex gpt-5-codex (medium) thought for 14s

d3.zoom and d3.brush still emit the same recursive update pattern they always have: when you programmatically drive one (e.g., zoomarea.call(axisZoom.transform, …)), D3 fires its listener with a fresh event whose sourceEvent points back to the initiating interaction. In v5 we relied solely on the sourceEvent.type check to bail out, but under v7 we added a couple of programmatic calls—resizeBrush() and the brush→zoom sync—that don’t come with a sourceEvent (or use a legacy event via the compat helpers). Without an explicit guard those updates bounce back and forth indefinitely.

let suppressBrush/suppressZoom—declared up top and used in resizeBrush() and brushed()/zoomed()—simply provide that guard:

  • When we move the brush ourselves (resizeBrush()), we set suppressBrush = true during the brush.call(brushObj.move, limits) call so the ensuing brushed listener exits immediately instead of trying to drive the zoom again (src/bgraph.js:1778-1790).
  • Similarly, inside brushed() we set suppressZoom = true around the zoomarea.call(axisZoom.transform, …) to keep zoomed() from reacting to our own update (src/bgraph.js:1834-1852).
  • Both listeners start by checking the corresponding flag (src/bgraph.js:1803-1804, src/bgraph.js:1833-1834).

So the booleans aren’t changing behavior when the user pans or zooms manually; they just prevent the two programmatic sync paths from triggering each other endlessly—especially important now that the compat layer sometimes feeds us “synthetic” events with no reliable sourceEvent.

Yeah, we could dodge the extra globals by leaning on state that already travels with the events:

  • Short-circuit via event.sourceEvent: Wrap the programmatic brush/zoom calls so you pass along a synthetic sourceEvent (e.g., {type: 'internal-brush-sync'}) and bail out when you see that token inside the listener. That keeps everything local to the handler instead of toggling shared flags.
  • Annotate the dispatched event: Instead of calling brushObj.move(...) directly, dispatch a CustomEvent with, say, detail: {internal: true}. Inside brushed()/zoomed() check event.detail?.internal and exit early. Works in the browser’s native event loop without introducing module-level state.
  • Track work-in-progress on the selection itself: You can stash a tiny symbol on the brush SVG group (brush.node().__internalSync = true) before the programmatic move and delete it in a finally. The handler reads the presence of that symbol to decide if it should return.

All of those keep the guard scoped to the interaction you’re managing, so we wouldn’t need suppressBrush/suppressZoom globals—the current approach just happened to be the quickest to drop in while refactoring.

That helper is the tiny guard inside the data-table click/edit path. When D3 v7 invokes our cell handlers it now passes the event first; some older code still expected this or the bare target. resolveDataTarget just normalizes whatever we get—explicit target, event.currentTarget, or the active element—into a DOM node so the downstream code can pull row IDs and indexes without blowing up. 23:41 Codex gpt-5-codex (medium) thought for 8s

Yeah. The data-table interactions (dataEdit, dataDelete, etc.) assume they’re handed a DOM node—the button or cell that was clicked—so they can walk to the parent row and extract the index. With D3 v7 every handler is called as (event, datum), so the “thing” our callbacks see is the event object instead of the node reference they used to rely on. resolveDataTarget is the tiny translator that turns whatever we get (explicit target, event.currentTarget, or the active element if we triggered it programmatically) back into the DOM node the rest of the code expects. Without it, those helpers try to call .parentElement on the event object and blow up.

You’re not misunderstanding—resolveDataTarget is basically a band‑aid because our handlers were written back when D3 called them as (datum, index) and we leaned on this implicitly. With D3 v7, every handler is (event, datum), so the quick fix was “look in the event, fall back to currentTarget/activeElement, and keep the downstream code untouched.”

If we’d rather not have that little shim, the clean approach is to update the table bindings so they hand the DOM node (or the event) straight through. For example:

…and then adjust dataEdit/dataDelete to use event.currentTarget (or just this when we call them). That keeps the codepaths explicit and makes resolveDataTarget unnecessary. I didn’t go that far originally because the helper was a fast way to keep the old logic working, but if we want to tidy it up, refactoring those handlers is the way to go.

On the pointerXY/dragCoord helpers:

  • pointerXY: We use it in dotAdded so the double-click handler works across both pointer-aware and older browsers. It prefers d3.pointer(event, node) (the v7 way), falls back to d3.mouse if available, and finally to a DOM-based coordinate if neither exists.

So both helpers are little compatibility shims to keep the drag and double-click flows working regardless of input modality or D3 internals.

why did that work for d3 v5? we need a better conceptual understanding of this v5->v7 upgrade. so far we're just making ad hoc patches as we notice things that are broken, it seems.
12:47 Codex gpt-5-codex (medium) thought for 17s

In D3 v5 most of the event plumbing looked very different:

  • Every handler was invoked as (datum, index) with the current event tucked away in the global d3.event. That meant the code could assume it was getting the *datum* in its first argument, and all the pointer info lived under that global.
  • d3.mouse(...) was the canonical way to get coordinates, and drag events exposed their position via d3.event.x and d3.event.y. The drag subject and source events were rarely used because the global event always carried the values.
  • Because dotAdded was wired both to real DOM events *and* fired programmatically, it often ran with d3.event still set from a previous interaction—hence bu.shn(d[1]) never saw undefined.

D3 v7 flipped that model:

  • Handlers are now (event, datum); D3 no longer mutates a global. If you call the handler yourself (or reference it from a timer), you’re now handing it an event object—or nothing at all—which is why showDotText suddenly saw missing data when we re-used it outside a “real” event.
  • d3.pointer(event, node) replaces d3.mouse, and drag coordinates live on the passed event (event.x/event.y, event.selection, etc.). If you ignore the event parameter, you simply lose the pointer.
  • We upgrade the graph from v5 to v7 in place, which re-exposed all the implicit assumptions: when we used legacy globals, the arrow functions never needed to pull currentTarget, suppressBrush relied on sourceEvent always being defined, and the showDotText path quietly depended on the old call shape.

So the “ad hoc patches” you’re seeing are really us re-aligning the code with the v7 world order:

  • Anywhere we previously ignored the event parameter, we now read it explicitly (drag handlers, zoom/brush, double-click).
  • Where we relied on d3.event or d3.mouse, we added shims (pointerXY, normalizeDragArgs) so the existing behavior survived while we exercised the v7 API (event, d3.pointer, event.selection).
  • Pieces like showDotText needed a guard only because we can now invoke it in contexts where the datum is absent—something v5’s implicit globals masked.

The good news is we’ve worked through the hot spots. The graph now functions under v7, and the remaining compatibility helpers are tiny and well-scoped. Whenever you’re ready, we can revisit each one and decide if we still need the fallback; but the key conceptual takeaway is that v7 expects handlers to use the event parameter directly, whereas v5 quietly supplied everything via d3.event.

  • Jumping to v6 first doesn’t really help. The hard breaking change you’re facing—loss of the global d3.event plus all the pointer helpers (d3.mouse, d3.touch)—arrived with v6. Moving to v6 would force the same refactor you need for v7, so you may as well aim straight for v7 and only do the churn once.

Prep Work On v5

Thanks for pushing back—that makes sense. Here are changes that keep the v5 code tidy but also line us up for a clean v7 jump:

  • Inject the event explicitly at the binding sites. For every handler today, define it as function onScroll(evt) { … } and wire it with zoomarea.on("wheel.scroll", function() { onScroll(d3.event); }, {passive:false}). That keeps the handler pure, removes hidden globals, and when you move to v7 you just switch the binding to zoomarea.on("wheel.scroll", (event) => onScroll(event), {passive:false}) without rewriting the handler body.
  • Centralize pointer math. Add a tiny pointer(evt, node) utility that the handlers call. Right now it can just return d3.mouse(node) (ignoring evt), but the helper gives you a single place to flip to d3.pointer(evt, node) in v7. Cleaner now, future-proof later.
  • Emit real DOM events when redispatching. Instead of cloning with new d3.event.constructor(d3.event.type, d3.event), build a WheelEvent/PointerEvent yourself and dispatch it. That reduces the weird dependency on D3’s internals immediately, and the same code works in v7.
  • Isolate zoom/brush state. Wrap the current d3.zoomTransform(…) and d3.event.sourceEvent access in helpers like currentTransform() and sourceType(evt). That makes the code easier to skim today and replaces every d3.event touch point with a function call you can adapt later.
  • Adopt module-friendly D3 usage. For any new work, import the specific subpackages (const {zoom, brush} = window.d3 today or, if you bundle, import {zoom} from 'd3-zoom'). V5 already supports modular builds, and moving this direction trims globals and makes the upgrade mostly about swapping import paths, not rewiring logic.

If we tighten those pieces up while still on v5, the later step is mostly just adjusting the event injection and switching pointer helpers—no shims, no ugly fallbacks.

can you read https://observablehq.com/@d3/d3v6-migration-guide and show me that you understand it?
21:12 Codex gpt-5-codex (medium) thought for 1h25m48s
  • D3 v6 modernizes the codebase: every package now ships ES2015+ syntax, so you’re expected to transpile if you still target legacy browsers. The default bundles dropped Bower; you use npm/CDNs like unpkg instead.
  • The headline breaking change is the event system. d3.event disappears; every listener now receives (event, datum) (index and group aren’t passed, so you reconstruct those as needed). This applies consistently across d3-selection, d3-brush, d3-drag, and d3-zoom, with the guide showing direct translations and even the destructuring pattern you can adopt (function zoomed({transform}) { … }).
  • Pointer helpers were consolidated: d3.mouse, d3.touch, d3.touches, and d3.clientPoint are gone, replaced by d3.pointer/d3.pointers. All of the examples show swapping the static helpers for the new call that takes the event object.
  • Deprecated modules were retired in favor of native or newer equivalents. d3-collection’s map, set, keys, values, entries, nest, and rollup become Map, Set, Object.*, d3.group, and d3.rollup/rollups, with the guide calling out how group results are now [key, values] tuples and how to destructure them.
  • Array utilities were renamed or tweaked: d3.histogram → d3.bin, d3.scan → d3.leastIndex (now returns -1 rather than undefined on failure), and the guide shows how that affects guard code.
  • Spatial work shifts from d3.voronoi to d3.Delaunay, with notes that you can still import the old module separately if you need the legacy API.
  • A few smaller but important API quirks: d3.interpolateTransformCss now insists on absolute units because it uses DOMMatrix, and d3-format formats negatives with the Unicode minus by default (you override via formatDefaultLocale).

That captures every section in the migration guide, plus the rationale/examples it provides for upgrading real code.

22:39 Codex gpt-5-codex (medium) thought for 10s
  • You already pull d3@^7.9.0 via npm for the Node side, so you’re paying the cost of that dependency anyway; serving that same build to the browser keeps the runtime in sync (no CDN stuck on v5 while package.json says v7).
  • Local hosting removes the external dependency—graphs keep working offline, you avoid TLS/hotlink hiccups, and you don’t have to trust future CDN redirects or outages.
  • It also makes upgrades deterministic: bump the npm version once, rebuild, and both server and browser code run the same bits without chasing a CDN query string.
  • The only extra work is wiring your build to ship node_modules/d3/dist/d3.min.js (or a tree‑shaken bundle) with the rest of your static assets; your existing gulp pipeline is already well-positioned to copy/minify that file.

    if (!event.sourceEvent) return;
    if (event.sourceEvent.type === "zoom") return;
    …
  }

right above const selection = event.selection; short-circuits the programmatic brush moves while still letting real pointer / wheel events drive the zoom. You won’t lose any functionality: explicit zoom commands (zoomDefault, zoomAll, button clicks) already set the domains before they invoke axisZoom.transform, and user drags still have a non-null sourceEvent.

Once that guard is in place, the infinite invert → transform → move cycle stops and the RangeError disappears.

Based on the current code in src/beebrain.js:719 and src/broad.js:1072, meandelt is the mean of consecutive day‑to‑day deltas after gap‑filling the processed data. Assuming kyoom=true, aggday="sum" (default for kyoom), and asof after day 5:

  • Raw daily sums: day1=1, day2=2, day4=1, day5=1
  • Kyoom cumulative data: day1=1, day2=3, day4=4, day5=5
  • Gap‑fill inserts day3 linearly: day3=3.5
  • gfdv = [1, 3, 3.5, 4, 5]

Given the current implementation, yes with a caveat. meandelt is the mean of consecutive differences on the gap-filled daily series (src/beebrain.js:719, src/broad.js:1072). For any sequence x0..xN, the mean of (x_i - x_{i-1}) is (xN - x0)/N, so intermediate values cancel. That means any fill (including repeating prev/next) leaves meandelt unchanged as long as you keep the same endpoints and the same number of daily steps. It changes only if the gap fill changes the number of inserted points or omits endpoints.

As of March 13, 2026, yes: Node 24 is the latest LTS and is in Active LTS; Node 22 is already in Maintenance LTS. I also ran the root quals locally on v24.8.0, and they passed.

For this repo, I would use ^24.0.0 (or equivalently >=24 <25) rather than open-ended >=24. The root manifest currently says >=22 in [package.json](/Users/dreeves/lab/road/package.json#L32), and [jsbrain_server/package.json](/Users/dreeves/lab/road/jsbrain_server/package.json) has no engines field. >=22 is already looser than parts of the current dependency tree: the root lockfile has packages requiring ^22.13.0 || >=24 at [package-lock.json](/Users/dreeves/lab/road/package-lock.json#L141), and jsbrain_server has ^22.12.0 || >=23 at [jsbrain_server/package-lock.json](/Users/dreeves/lab/road/jsbrain_server/package-lock.json#L2298).

^24 means “24.x only”. >=24 means “24 and every future major”. So the reason to use >= is only if you intentionally want “minimum supported version” semantics. For an app repo like this, I’d usually prefer ^24.0.0 because it fails loudly on Node 25/26 instead of claiming support before you’ve rerun quals there. If your real goal is standardizing the dev toolchain, npm’s devEngines is a better fit than engines, since engines is advisory unless engine-strict is enabled.

Sources: Node release schedule, npm package.json engines / devEngines, npm semver caret ranges

Yes — found one, and it's squarely user-visible: bu.shn, the number formatter, unambiguously misrounds positive numbers, while formatting the same negative numbers correctly. The sign asymmetry is the smoking gun: shn(x) and shn(-x) should never disagree in magnitude, so one of each pair is provably wrong — and in every case it's the positive one.

Two distinct defects, verified against the actual module:

| call | shows | should show (= what -x correctly gives) |
|---|---|---|
| shn(0.46, 3,1) | 0.4 | 0.5 |
| shn(0.49, 3,1) | 0.4 | 0.5 |
| shn(9.01, 4,2) | 9 | 9.01 |
| shn(9.95, 4,2) | 9.9 | 9.95 |
| shn(99.9, 4,2) | 100 | 99.9 |
| shn(999.13, 4,2) | 1000 | 999.1 |

Scanning x = 0.01…999.99: 9,275 values misformat at t=4,d=2, 2,757 at t=3,d=1. (Defaults t=10,d=5 are clean, so hover text and the road-editor table escape it.)

Root causes, both in [butil.js](src/butil.js#L398-L420):

  1. [butil.js:403](src/butil.js#L403) — the // Hack to prevent incorrect rounding line if (vm >= 4.5 && vm < 4.9999999) v = floor(v). The window is meant (I believe) to catch floating-point noise around exact halves, but it's ~0.5 wide instead of ~1e-7 wide, so any value whose scaled last digit lands in [.45, .50) gets floored: 0.46 → 0.4. Negative values dodge it because vm += 10 shifts them out of the window — hence the asymmetry.
  2. [butil.js:418-420](src/butil.js#L418-L420) — the floor(xn) === 9 || 99 || 999 special case formats via x.toPrecision(k) where k is a count of *decimal digits* but toPrecision takes *significant figures*. So anything in [9,10), [99,100), [999,1000) gets k sig figs instead: 9.01 → "9", 99.9 → "100".

Where users see it: ratesum ([beebrain.js:1465-1472](src/beebrain.js#L1465-L1472)) is built from bu.shn(rate, 4, 2) — a goal with rate 9.95/week displays "9.9 per week", 99.9/month displays "100 per month". Also statsum's vini/vcur/vfin lines. (graphsum/limsum go through conservaround instead since quantum defaults to 1e-5, so they're unaffected.)

Why I stopped here instead of fixing: the minimal fix — tighten the hack window to ~1e-7 and make the 9/99/999 branch use xn.toPrecision(t) like the general path — changes rendered numbers on existing production graphs, which automon will flag, and there's one semantic question only you can answer: exact halves like 0.45 currently round *down* to 0.4 (and would keep doing so under the tightened window); school rounding says 0.5. Say the word and I'll do it red/green — quals for the table above first, then the fix.

Why your graph shifted down by a constant amount: on any past day where the road's rate was lower than rfin — a break, a flat segment, weekends-off, or any datapoint before tini (the pre-road segment has slope 0) — that day's sum is now capped lower, possibly at 0. Since this is a kyoom goal, one day aggregating lower shifts every subsequent cumulative point down by that same difference. In your screenshots the whole purple line is down ~70 (about one day's rate) and the day-to-day increments are unchanged, so the affected day is at or before Dec 25, outside the visible window — the visible road is constant-rate, so look earlier in the goal for a flat/reduced-rate stretch with data on it.

|---|---|---|---|---|

| Dec 24 | 90 | 65 | 245 | 180 |
| … | | | *every later point −65* | |

One boundary detail confirmed in that run: a knot belongs to the segment that *starts* there (findSeg returns the later segment), so a datapoint on the day a flat segment begins gets rate 0, while a datapoint on the day the break ends gets the resumed rate.

Your instinct is right, and the good news is your desired workflow has a name — trunk-based with the working tree as the review inbox — and it's almost exactly what we've already built. Let me lay out the mental model, then close the one gap.

The model you're describing:

  • The repo sits on master, forever. Branches never enter your consciousness.
  • Agents are typists: they edit files in the working tree, nothing else. Every change they make shows up in VS Code's Source Control panel as an uncommitted diff against master.
  • The commit is your approval stamp. You peruse diffs, discard hunks you dislike (VS Code's discard = your git, unrestricted), stage what you like, write the message that matters to you, and Commit & Sync. Done.

What already enforces this (from today's lockdown, which turns out to fit this philosophy better than "block the mess" — it *defines the contract*):

  • Agents can't branch, switch, or make worktrees → work can only land in the visible working tree.
  • Agents can't git add or git commit → nothing ever gets staged behind your back, and no commit message in your history is ever anyone's but yours.
  • Agents can't git stash → no more changes vanishing into stash@{0}: stupid ai.
  • Agents keep git diff/git log → they can still see their own work and your history, which they genuinely need.

The one gap, given your goal: background/queued sessions currently default to working in an isolated worktree — meaning their changes would *not* appear in your VS Code diffs, which is the opposite of what you want. Yesterday's revelation cuts the other way now: you don't want background isolation "cleaned up better," you want it off. That's worktree: {bgIsolation: "none"} — background agents edit the same working copy you're looking at. Applying it:

Memory saved. To recap the thinking in one paragraph: what you want isn't really a git policy, it's a division of labor — agents produce diffs, you produce commits. The config now encodes exactly that: git is read-only for agents (diff/log), background sessions write to the same working tree you review in VS Code, and the commit step — message and all — is physically reserved for you. The only ceremony left in your life is the one-time cleanup of the current branch situation, and after that "sync to master" is just the Commit & Sync button, because you'll already *be* on master, always.

Good question to end the audit with — let me gather actual measurements rather than speculate. Three areas look promising: the jsbrain render pipeline (the log showed page *creation* at 830ms vs 34ms for the actual render), the page weight of the editor app (it ships unminified sources), and the drag-path DOM work. Starting with the renderer lifecycle:

The renderer pools page *slots*, but let me see what the 830ms "Page creation" timer actually covers and how repeat requests behave:

The steady-state cost is the screenshot step: 548ms of the ~600ms total. Looking at what that step does:

gm isn't on this shell's PATH (the server process found it fine). Locating and timing:

Efficiency findings, all measured rather than guessed, ranked by impact. I haven't changed any code — say which of these you want and I'll implement them.

Server-side graph rendering (jsbrain_server) — the big wins

1. The page pool's 10-second idle timeout forces the cold path constantly. Measured: a cold render pays 825ms of page creation; a warm one pays 18ms — a 45× difference — but [renderer.js:334](jsbrain_server/renderer.js#L334) closes idle tabs after just 10 seconds. Unless production traffic arrives more than once per 10 seconds, most renders pay the cold price. Raising that constant to minutes (or pinning one always-warm page) is a one-line change; the cost is one idle Chrome tab's memory.

2. Two sequential ImageMagick subprocesses eat ~75% of warm render time. Steady-state timing: 18ms page creation + 18ms render + 548ms screenshot step, of which the thumbnail crop/remap (~200ms) and the full-PNG palette remap (~258ms) run back-to-back ([renderer.js:268-297](jsbrain_server/renderer.js#L268-L297)). Two options: parallelizing them saves ~200ms (they'd need the remap to write to its own temp file instead of overwriting the input the thumbnail reads); replacing gm with sharp (libvips, in-process) would do both ops in tens of milliseconds, saving ~400ms per render, at the cost of a new native dependency. Side observation: the gm package is actually finding ImageMagick v7's deprecated convert shim on this machine, which is worth knowing about for env brittleness.

3. generate.html fetches d3 from a CDN on every cold navigation. That's a network RTT inside the cold path and a hard runtime dependency on jsdelivr, complete with its own failure branch ("Could not load d3! No internet?"). Serving the local minified copy the way every other script on that page is served removes both.

The graph editor page (client)

4. The production page ships ~1.4MB of JavaScript, unminified, in ~13 requests. [grapheditor.ejs](views/grapheditor.ejs) loads src/*.js directly (825KB) plus *unminified* d3 from the CDN (573KB). Gulp already builds exactly what's needed: bsbpack.min.js (171KB, covers polyfit through bsandbox) + grapheditor.min.js (14KB) + minified moment/moment-timezone (98KB) + d3.v7.min.js (273KB) ≈ 560KB — a 2.5× cut using artifacts that already exist, before compression. Related: the express server has no compression middleware, so all of this goes over the wire raw unless Render's proxy gzips it (worth checking); minified + gzipped this page would be roughly 200KB. The tradeoff is debuggability of prod, which is presumably why it serves src/ — your call whether that tradeoff is still earning its keep.

5. Every goal load runs three full beebrain pipelines. loadGoals feeds the same JSON serially to the graph, editor, and sandbox engines, rendering hidden tabs included. It's ~20ms per engine on test goals but scales with data size, so it triples the load time of exactly the goals that are already slow. Lazy per-tab loading would fix it but changes behavior (first switch to a tab would show a beat of loading), so I'd want your sign-off before touching it.

Retraction

6. tableUpdateOnDrag is fine — downgrading my own earlier flag. I'd flagged the full-table rebuild + forced reflow per drag frame as a potential jank source. Measured on an 82-knot matrix: p50/p90 frame gaps are identical with the option off vs on (16.6/16.7ms — locked 60fps), max frame occasionally 21→29ms. No action warranted; the review finding can be considered closed.

Small fry, for completeness: /src and /lib are served with ETags but no Cache-Control: max-age, so repeat visits pay a conditional-request RTT per file (compounding with #4's 13 requests); and the qual suite runs its browser quals serially (~2min) which could parallelize, but that's dev-only time.

The likeliest bundle if you want my recommendation: #1 + #2's parallelization + #3 are all small, low-risk, and together take warm renders from ~600ms to ~400ms and cold ones from ~1.6s to well under a second; #4 is the biggest user-facing win but deserves a deliberate decision about serving minified code.

is remapftmp ok as a const?
17:46 Claude Code claude-fable-5 thought for 1m26s · 1m47s wall-clock time

Yes — remapftmp is assigned once and never reassigned (its only other appearances are reads: the .write() target and the two fs calls), and unlike its neighbors it doesn't need var's function-scope hoisting: imgftmp/svgftmp/thmftmp are declared inside if (graphit) but read after that block closes (the fs.existsSync(imgftmp) rename), so they lean on var hoisting when graphit is false, whereas remapftmp's declaration and both uses all live inside the same block. I used var purely to match those neighbors, but const is strictly safer here — any future reassignment becomes an immediate loud error, which is exactly the failure mode this file's history argues for. Changing it and re-verifying:

Confirmed good. const remapftmp renders cleanly (no error, all four outputs produced, pixel signature identical to the previous renders, screenshot step still ~340ms) and the static-analysis qual passes over the file.

To recap the reasoning since you asked: const is right for remapftmp because it's never reassigned and every use sits inside the same if (graphit) block as the declaration. The one thing to *not* do is extend that to its neighbors — imgftmp, svgftmp, and thmftmp are also declared inside if (graphit) but imgftmp is read after that block closes, so those three depend on var's function-scope hoisting (when graphit is false, fs.existsSync(undefined) quietly returns false). Converting them would take a small restructure, not a keyword swap.

Fixed, with the regression pinned down precisely — and good news: it wasn't from this week's work.

Root cause: commit 480ab4a ("Add asserts per anti-robustness principle", March 12) changed butil.loadJSON to reject(err) when a response fails to parse as JSON, but neither caller was ever updated to handle rejection. So any non-JSON response — classically /getgoaljson/<goal> with a dead session, where the server 302s the XHR to the login page and it comes back as <!DOCTYPE html>… — escaped as exactly your console error, and because everything after the bare await was skipped, the three "loading…" overlays stayed stranded. bgraph.loadGoalFromURL had it even worse: its loading guard flag never reset, permanently bricking that graph instance until page reload.

Your stale-server hypothesis is an alternate route to the same place — an Express 404 HTML page instead of a login page — which is presumably what you hit. Either way it's the same code path, and since it's been live since March, production users whose sessions expired mid-edit have likely been hitting it quietly too.

Fix: restored loadJSON's original contract — resolve(null) on parse failure — because both callers already have designed error paths for null ("Could not load goal file." overlay, failed-load logging); rejecting bought nothing those paths don't do, and broke both callers. The replacement comment documents the contract and names 480ab4a explicitly so a future anti-robustness sweep doesn't re-break it. 23:03 Claude Code claude-fable-5 thought for 4m57s · 5m52s wall-clock time

The ghost-undo nit — where a stale matrix-cell focus re-commits after undoAll(). Before deciding on a fix, let me read the full rdFocus lifecycle and what the undo family actually does:

All three flows verified. Recompiling and adding the changelog line:

Ghost-undo bug fixed, red-green, with the fix landing at the mechanism's root rather than patching undo.

The mechanism: tableFocusOut commits a cell edit whenever the cell's text differs from rdFocus.oldText, a cache taken at focus-in (or re-armed after an Enter commit). Undo, redo, undo-all, and goal reloads all rewrite the table's cell text programmatically *without* touching that cache — so a cell still holding focus (which it does after an Enter commit) compares its rewritten text against the stale cache on the next focus change and manufactures an edit the user never made.

The fix: two lines at the single chokepoint every programmatic table rewrite flows through — updateTableValues now voids the editing session (rdFocus.field/oldText = null) before rewriting cell texts. That covers undo, redo, undo-all, *and* goal switches in one move, with no special-casing of any of them. Normal editing is unaffected because both legitimate commit paths re-establish their state after the rewrite: the Enter path re-arms oldText after its commit chain runs, and the focusout path has already read the text it's committing.

Verified end-to-end in the browser, beyond the suite:

  • Edit a cell and click away without Enter → commits (slope 3, undo count 1) — the fix doesn't eat legitimate focusout commits.
  • The replicata itself: edit, undoAll, click elsewhere → count stays 0, road untouched (pre-fix: count 1).
  • Enter-commit, keep typing in the same cell, click away → both edits land (slope 4, count 2) — the post-Enter re-arm still works.

The new qual pins the replicata permanently (it failed with {"undocnt":"1"} before the fix, exactly the "Graph Editor (1)" ghost from the screenshots), the full suite is green, and lib is recompiled. Diff for review: src/bgraph.js (+7 comment/reset lines in updateTableValues), quals/claude_quals.js (+20), CHANGELOG.

Reviewing the recent work with fresh eyes... found it, and glaring is the word: reflected XSS through the deep-link params. The template emits goal and wanted into an inline <script> via <%- JSON.stringify(...) %> — raw output. JSON.stringify escapes quotes but *not* </script>, and req.params arrive URL-decoded, so a crafted link like /bob/%3C%2Fscript%3E%3Cscript%3E… breaks out of the script tag and runs attacker JS with bob's session. Proving it end-to-end first, then fixing:the </ gets escaped to <\/ in a JSON string context, which HTML-parsers treat as a non-closing sequence.

Confirmed — and it's serious. JSON.stringify does not escape </script>, and the template emits the deep-link params raw into an inline script. Writing the qual that proves the exploit first:

Exploit reproduced — pwned: "number" means the attacker's script ran. Now the fix:

Green — payload now inert. Continuing the careful review for the same class of issue elsewhere:

All remaining <%- emissions are our own markup helpers (safe). Two more hardening items the review turned up — the login-redirect stash and URL building:

The glaring thing was a reflected XSS I introduced with the deep links. Found, proven, fixed, and qualed.

The vulnerability. The template hands the deep-link params to the client through an inline <script> via <%- JSON.stringify(goal) %>. JSON.stringify escapes quotes but leaves </script> completely intact, and Express hands you req.params already URL-decoded. So a link like graph.beeminder.com/bob/%3C%2Fscript%3E%3Cscript%3E… closes the script tag and runs the attacker's JavaScript in the victim's page — with their session, their token, their goals. Mailing that link to a logged-in Beeminder user is the whole exploit. My qual reproduced it outright: pwned: "number" — the injected script executed.

The fix. A jsval() helper in the template that does JSON.stringify(v).replace(/</g, '\\u003c'), used for all three inline-script values. Escaping < (not just the </script> sequence) kills the entire class — script-tag breakout, <!-- comment tricks, everything. Rendering the payload now yields the inert string "\u003c/script>\u003cscript>alert(1)…", and the browser sees no second script tag.

Quals added (red-first, both):

  • A runtime XSS qual: a page rendered with a hostile goalname must not execute anything — window.pwned stays undefined, the payload remains a plain string, and the user just gets the no-such-graph banner. It failed loudly before the fix.
  • A structural qual on the template: zero raw <%- JSON.stringify emissions may exist, so the next person who adds a value to that script block can't reintroduce the hole by reflex.

Two more things the review turned up, both hardened:

  • The login return-to stash was req.session.wanted = req.originalUrl — a request-controlled string later fed straight to resp.redirect(). Browsers won't send an absolute-form request target, so this wasn't practically exploitable, but it's an open-redirect shape. It's now rebuilt from the route params ("/" + encodeURIComponent(username) + "/" + encodeURIComponent(goalname)), so the redirect target is provably a local two-segment path.
  • updateURL() now percent-encodes the username and slug it writes into the address bar, so an exotic character in a slug can't corrupt the URL.

I checked every other <%- in the views: all remaining ones emit our own markup helpers (the chip partials, the undo SVGs), no user data. login.ejs and sandbox.ejs use escaped <%= throughout. Full suite green, gulp compile clean.

Worth saying plainly: this was my bug, introduced two turns ago, and I shipped it past my own "review carefully" pass. The lesson I'd encode is that *any* new value crossing from a URL into an inline script deserves the same reflex as SQL — which is now what the structural qual enforces mechanically.

is the reserved prefix the best solution? could we also just disallow conflicting usernames?
14:58 Claude Code claude-fable-5 thought for 1m43s

They solve different halves of the problem, so "just" disallowing usernames wouldn't be enough on its own — but it changes what the best app-side fix is.

What username reservation fixes: no real person can ever be shadowed by a route. That's worth doing on the beeminder.com side regardless (and I'd guess most of these are already unregistrable or nonexistent). But the conflict surface is smaller than it looks. Because the static mounts fall through on a miss, a user actually named data or tutorial deep-links fine today unless a file with exactly their goal's name exists. The only route that *hard*-shadows a deep link is GET /getgoaljson/:goal — a user named getgoaljson — because it's the one other two-segment GET route. Everything else (/login/foo, /editor/foo, …) falls through to the deep-link route and works.

What it doesn't fix: the 404 wart. Even if no user can be named src, a request for /src/nonexistent.js still arrives, still matches /:username/:goalname, and still gets a 200 HTML page for a user that can't exist. The fix for that has to live in this app.

For the app side, I think there's something better than a reserved-prefix list: validate the two segments against what usernames and goal slugs can actually be. If I'm right that both are limited to [a-zA-Z0-9_-] (you'd know the exact Rails rules), then the handler calls next() for anything that couldn't possibly be a name, and Express 404s it. That kills essentially every asset-shaped request in one stroke — /src/foo.js, /lib/x.css, /favicon.ico/…, /wp-admin/setup.php — because file requests virtually always contain a dot. And it's not a special-case list, it's input validation: the route only claims paths that could denote a user's goal, which is the anti-robustness posture (reject impossible input loudly) rather than a magic enumeration of sibling routes that has to be maintained as routes get added. A reserved-prefix list, by contrast, starts at src, lib, data and honestly should grow to every route name to be consistent — that's the smell.

The two combined give a clean division: the grammar guard here makes non-name paths 404, and reserving the route names on beeminder.com (really just getgoaljson strictly, the rest as insurance against future routes) guarantees no person is ever shadowed.

One caveat on verification: the guard lives in server.js, which the qual suite doesn't boot, so I'd verify it with curl the way I did the other server probes rather than with a qual.

If you confirm the username/slug charset, I'll add the guard to the deep-link route and curl-verify the matrix (missing assets → 404, real-shaped names → editor, encoded-slash cases still safe).

what can we do about this and is it specific to dev:

GET http://localhost:3001/d 404 (Not Found)
Connecting to 'http://localhost:3001/.well-known/appspecific/com.chrome.devtools.json' violates the following Content Security Policy directive: "default-src 'none'". The request has been blocked. Note that 'connect-src' was not explicitly set, so 'default-src' is used as a fallback.
15:16 Claude Code claude-fable-5 thought for 1m29s

Both lines are dev-only noise, and neither is caused by the URL feature or the new guard. Here's what's actually happening:

The CSP message is Chrome DevTools' "automatic workspace folders" feature. When DevTools is open on a *localhost* origin (it's gated to loopback origins, so this never fires in production), Chrome probes /.well-known/appspecific/com.chrome.devtools.json to ask the server "should I map these files to a local checkout for editing?" The CSP that blocks it isn't ours — this app sends no CSP header at all. It's Express's built-in 404 handler (finalhandler), which hardens its generated error pages with Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'. So the sequence was: you landed on a 404 page (/d), DevTools ran its probe in that page's context, and the 404 page's own CSP blocked the fetch. On real app pages the probe just 404s without the CSP complaint.

The /d 404 is a plain no-route-matches 404 — one segment, so it never even reaches the deep-link route (and predates the guard in behavior). If you didn't deliberately visit /d, the usual culprit is the omnibox: Chrome prefetches partially-typed URLs, so typing localhost:3001/de… can fire a request for /d mid-keystroke.

What you can do, in order of my preference:

  1. Nothing. It only appears on dev 404 pages with DevTools open. There's no code change here that isn't adding a route to appease a browser probe.
  2. Silence it browser-side: DevTools → Settings → uncheck "Automatic workspace folders". Kills the probe entirely.
  3. Lean into it: serve that well-known path in dev with {"workspace": {"root": "/Users/dreeves/lab/road", "uuid": "<any-fixed-uuid>"}}. Chrome then offers to connect the repo as a DevTools workspace, and CSS/JS edits made in DevTools write straight to your working tree — plausibly nice for tweaking grapheditor.css live, since the app serves src/ unbuilt. But it's a route that exists only to please Chrome, so I wouldn't add it unless you'd actually use that workflow.

Small surface, lots of correctness details to get just right: yoog first (so truncated tabs still show the goal), an unsaved-edits bullet that mirrors the beforeunload condition exactly, no title churn during drags (Safari throttles replaceState but not document.title), and the base name read from the template's <title> so there's one source of truth.

The small thing: browser tab titles that tell the truth. A tab now reads d/pushups · Beeminder Visual Graph Editor, and grows a bullet — ● d/pushups · … — the moment the editor holds an unsaved edit, shedding it on undo or submit. Five goals in five tabs are now tellable apart, and the one you'd lose work in announces itself.

The details that took the extra mile, since each had a wrong-but-plausible alternative:

  • Yoog first, app name last. Browsers truncate tab labels from the right, so leading with "Beeminder Visual Graph Editor" would make every tab identical precisely when you have too many tabs — the only time titles matter.
  • The bullet's condition is exactly the beforeunload warning's condition (editor.undoBufferState().undo > 0), not a parallel notion of "dirty". The tab marker and the are-you-sure dialog can never disagree, and it works in View mode too if edits are pending — which the qual proves incidentally, since it dials the rate while the View tab is active.
  • Title updates ride editorChanged, not replaceState. Dragging the red line fires road-change events continuously, and Safari hard-throttles history.replaceState (~100 per 30s) while document.title is free — so the URL updates only on goal/mode changes, as before, and the title updates on every edit. That constraint is written into the comment at [grapheditor.js:60-71](src/grapheditor.js#L60-L71).
  • BASETITLE is read from the template's <title> rather than duplicating the string in JS, so the page keeps one source of truth for its own name (and your exact "Beeminder Visual Graph Editor" copy is reused byte-for-byte, never retyped).
  • The yoog logic got extracted into curYoog(), which updateURL now shares — the address bar and the tab can't drift apart, and local pages (whose "goals" are file paths) keep a plain title but still get the unsaved bullet, which is meaningful there too.

That makes the caption and the graph agree for the whole time the slide is up, kills the main reason anyone would want replay, and adds no UI. It touches the anim script's step order (same kind of surgery as the edge-skating fix, captions untouched).

can you give me a concise explanation of the anim array so i can decide how to tweak some of these timings?
18:58 Claude Code claude-fable-5 thought for 32s

The anim array is a flat list of steps, each [delay, action]:

[s*30, ()=>gr.animYBR(true)],   // do the action, then wait s*30 ms

Timing: s is the global speed knob (const s = 100 near the top). Delay = s × n milliseconds, so s*3 = 300ms, s*30 = 3s, s*0 = no pause. The delay comes *after* its action — it's the gap before the next step runs. Cranking s down speeds up the whole show uniformly; editing an individual step's multiplier tunes just that beat.

Actions: gr.msg("...") shows a caption; bs.newData(v,"") enters a datapoint today; bs.nextDay advances a day; bs.newRate(r) re-dials the rate in units/day (takes effect a week out); gr.animYBR/animData/animBuf/animBux/animHor(true|false) switch the highlight pulses on and off — so the delay on a pulse-on step is how long the pulse shows before its off step.

Chapters: the engine derives them by scanning for gr.msg — a chapter is a caption plus every step until the next caption. Next performs one chapter at these authored delays; Prev replays the prefix with all delays skipped, then performs the target chapter. So your timings only ever matter *within* a chapter's performance.

Two consequences worth knowing when tweaking:

  1. The delay on a gr.msg step is the beat between the caption appearing and its illustration starting (e.g. [s*0, msg] → illustration starts instantly; the title card's s*20 → 2s hold).
  2. The delay on a chapter's *last* step isn't dead time — play() waits it out before the chapter counts as landed (counter flips, caption settles, buttons calm down). Nothing visual happens during it, so trailing delays are usually the first thing to cut to make chapters feel snappier. The title card's s*20 is the standout example: Prev-to-title holds "playing" for 2 idle seconds.

What the bug actually is

There is no single akrasia horizon; there are (at least) three definitions that disagree, and #232 is the visible seam between them. Writing T for calendar-today in the goal's timezone, and noting that asof (the bb file's "logical today", from TimeUtils.nowstamp) equals T before the deadline but T+1 after it:

| Enforcer | Locked window (dates where easing is rejected) |
|---|---|
| Rails legal_road_change_or_err, before 2026-06-26 | T through T+7 inclusive |
| Rails, current master (commit 5f469b4e, "Fix off-by-one in API akrasia-horizon road check", citing gissue 5447) | T through T+6; first legal easier day is T+7, matching take-a-break |
| Graph editor client, isRoadValid at [bgraph.js:2039](src/bgraph.js#L2039) | asof through asof+6, closed interval — both endpoints checked |
| The drawn dashed line / pink zone | at asof+6 ([beebrain.js:1686](src/beebrain.js#L1686), [bgraph.js:539](src/bgraph.js#L539)) |

  2. Pre-deadline goals: the dashed line is drawn at T+6, one day before the first legal easier day (T+7). Validation happens to agree with the server, but the picture says "free past this line" while the line's own day plus nothing-until-tomorrow is locked. cpcallen's expectation was set by this drawing.

The correct unifying rule is: horizon = T+7 where T is calendar-today in the goal's tz, deadline-agnostic; draw the line and pink zone edge there; forbid easing on dates strictly before it. Paste-ready summary for #232

**Investigation summary (2026-07-15, via Claude)**

TLDR: This bug had a server half and a client half. The server half -- the off-by-one that rejected the original replicata above -- was fixed in beeminder/beeminder@5f469b4e (2026-06-26, "Fix off-by-one in API akrasia-horizon road check", via beeminder/beeminder#5447). What remains is the client half in this repo: the graph editor draws and enforces its own, slightly different horizon. Fixing that closes this gissue plus #258, and finishes #280.

## The three horizons

Let T = calendar-today in the goal's timezone. The bb param `asof` is the daystamp of the beeminder-day in progress: T before the deadline, T+1 after it. The rule everyone should agree on (per take-a-break, and now codified in `legal_road_change_or_err`): the red line may not get easier on any of the 7 dates {T, ..., T+6}; T+7 -- the akrasia horizon -- is the first date it legally may.

| Enforcer | Locked dates |
|---|---|
| Rails `legal_road_change_or_err`, pre-fix | {T..T+7} -- one day too many; caused this gissue, #280, and beeminder#5447 |
| Rails, current master | {T..T+6}, matching `take_a_break`'s gate of `brk_start >= daysnap(now + 1.week)` |
| Graph editor client (`isRoadValid`, src/bgraph.js) | [asof, asof+6], closed interval, anchored to asof instead of T |
| Drawn dashed line / pink zone edge | asof+6 (beebrain.js: "draw the akrasia horizon 6 days out") |

Consequences, now that the Rails fix is in:

* **Before the deadline** (asof = T): client validation matches the server exactly, but the dashed line is drawn at T+6, one day before the true horizon. The picture says "free past this line" while the first free date is a day past the line. This is what made the original report so maddening.
* **After the deadline** (asof = T+1): the line lands at T+7, the right place -- but the closed-interval check forbids easing AT T+7, which the server now allows. The editor disables Submit ("Bright red line can't be easier within the akrasia horizon!") for perfectly legal changes. That's Mary's report in #258 and Emerald's notes above.

## Recommended fix (this repo)

1. Define the horizon once: hor = T+7, with T = calendar-today in `gol.timezone`. The bb file already ships `timezone` (currently ignored, beebrain.js ~line 180) and moment-timezone is already loaded on the editor page, so the client can compute T live -- recompute inside `isRoadValid` so the check self-heals if the editor sits open across midnight, instead of freezing at page-load asof.
2. Make `isRoadValid` check exactly the server's window: easier at any date in {T..T+6} means invalid; easing AT the drawn line (T+7) becomes legal, matching Rails and take-a-break, in both pre- and post-deadline cases.
3. Draw the dashed line and pink-zone right edge at T+7.
4. Consider matching the server's epsilon (client uses 1e-6, server 1e-9; deltas in between are client-silent, server-rejected).
5. Quals for pre- and post-deadline cases (`genStats` takes an injectable clock, so no clock-mocking heroics needed).
6. Verify end-to-end against a real goal, once before and once after the deadline: everything the editor allows, the API accepts, and vice versa. Also confirm beeminder/beeminder@5f469b4e is deployed.

Follow-up, not blocking: the bb outputs `pinkzone` and `rah` are anchored at asof+7 (a third variant of the horizon); unify or explicitly punt.

## Gissue bookkeeping

* #258: same root cause; merge into this one. Mary's half is the post-deadline client bug; Lanthala's half was never replicated and is plausibly mooted by the Rails fix.
* #280: replicata already fixed server-side by the Rails commit; the client fix closes the remaining warn-mismatch class.
* NOT this bug despite the resemblance: #336 and possibly #196 hit the *other* Rails check ("cannot bring end date closer if it is inside the akrasia horizon"), which fires even when the change makes the goal strictly harder -- separate Rails-side question. #196 also smells of 2-of-3 row-inference rounding. #236 and #187 are separate.

## Open question (Rails-side)

Anchoring to calendar-today is slightly leaky for after-midnight deadlines: at 1am with a 3am deadline, the in-progress date is already outside the locked window, so a roadall change could ease today's obligation two hours before its deadline. take-a-break shares the same anchor, so they're at least consistent with each other. Probably wants its own gissue.

  1. Prev is the worst case. For a chapter with a dozen 300ms steps, that's several seconds of the counter appearing frozen after you clicked Prev.

So each click of Next/Prev does move you exactly one chapter — the numbering does correspond to clicks eventually — but the displayed number trails by the length of the animation, which reads as broken.

The fix matching your expectation is small: make refreshControls() display dest+1 instead of cur-based math, and call refreshControls() from poke() (which covers both buttons plus the arrow keys) so it fires the instant dest moves. Want me to make that change?

The refactor is done and verified. The score is now a flat list of actions, exactly as you sketched, and the whole thing got about 80 lines shorter even after adding blank lines between chapters.

The vocabulary (defined at [tutorial.html:95-121](quals/tutorial.html#L95-L121)):

  • wait — chapter boundary; the driver recognizes it by identity. You write it bare (wait,), but I defined it as () => wait — it returns itself — so wait() works identically if fingers type that.
  • sleep(ms) — a beat as its own action, which no-ops when rushing or when restaging history for a backward seek. That let the rush/delay logic move out of the driver: play() is now just "await every action in the chapter."
  • banner(str) — your caption sugar, plus animYBR(b), animData(b), etc. as action factories. This killed the gr shim object entirely — the score no longer needs a fake graph interface.
  • data(x), day, rate(r) — sugar for the sandbox calls.
  • seq(ms, ...actions) — the one extra nicety: a uniform-tempo run, each action trailed by sleep(ms), spread into the score. So a chapter now reads like:
animYBR(false),
banner("Add new data for what you're beeminding"),

does it ever make sense to have a delay right before a HUP?
14:35 Claude Code claude-fable-5 thought for 56s

No — a beat immediately before a HUP is invisible, so it never earns its keep. By the time the beat runs, the chapter's last real action has already rendered; all the beat does is keep the driver officially "playing" a bit longer before it goes idle at the HUP. Nothing observable hangs on that: the counter already flipped at click time (it tracks dest), the buttons are never disabled mid-play, and if you click Next during the trailing beat, poke() cancels it anyway — so the experience is byte-for-byte identical with or without it. Same logic applies to a beat at the very end of the score.

Two corollaries:

  1. Riffle's trailing beat is self-neutralizing at chapter ends. Since riffle trails *every* action with a beat, any riffle that ends a chapter contributes one of these inert beats. That's harmless, and it's why you could safely drop the last beat when hand-expanding a riffle before a HUP, like you did in the derail chapter.
  1. Your current score has two explicit inert ones you could prune if you want zero dead weight: the 600 after the derail day (day, 600, // derail right before its HUP) and the 1000 after rate(2) at the end of the akrasia-horizon chapter. Purely cosmetic either way.

The one future scenario where trailing beats would start meaning something: an auto-advance/kiosk mode that plays through HUPs on a timer. Then "dwell time before moving on" becomes real, and you'd want them back.

oh, yeah, if kiosk mode means the HUPs are just ignored, then i guess we do want pauses before every HUP, right? and i think what you were saying is that hitting next (or prev) aborts so it doesn't matter if a pause is still running when a HUP happens. true?
14:52 Claude Code claude-fable-5 thought for 36s

True on both, with one refinement on the kiosk part.

On the abort behavior: yes, exactly. A click on Next or Prev cuts any in-flight beat short — poke() resolves the pending nap immediately — so a trailing pause never costs the human anything. Slight reframe of the wording: a HUP never "happens while a pause is running," because HUP isn't an action that fires — it's just the boundary marker the driver comes to rest at after the chapter's actions (trailing pause included) finish. But your conclusion is right: trailing beats are free from the human's perspective, whether they've finished, are mid-flight when clicked, or get skipped entirely during a multi-chapter rush.

On kiosk mode: you'd want dwell time at every boundary, yes — otherwise a chapter like "These are your datapoints" would flash its pulse on and the next chapter would immediately turn it off, with no time to absorb anything. But I'd argue against authoring that as explicit pauses before every HUP. The cleaner design: kiosk mode doesn't *ignore* HUPs, it *reinterprets* them — each HUP becomes "linger N milliseconds, then continue," with one global knob for N (or a reading-time heuristic based on the banner length). That's better on three counts:

  1. The score stays exactly as it is — no dead-weight beats to maintain in eighteen places, no drift between the two modes.
  2. Dwell time is one number instead of eighteen, and tuning "the kiosk feels rushed" is a one-line change.
  3. If the HUP-dwell is implemented as a nap, a walk-up human clicking Next aborts it just like any beat — so the kiosk gracefully hands control to a person and the same score serves both modes with zero changes.

HUP already means "the human absorbs the scene here"; kiosk mode just substitutes a timer for the human at exactly those spots. If you ever want it, it's a small addition to the driver — happy to build it when you do.

That's consistent with how this whole file works: you've been hand-tuning an accelerando into the data entry chapter; boundary dwells are the same kind of authorial decision.

The clincher is that your version needs zero new vocabulary: bare numbers and HUP already exist, so "beat, then HUP" expresses per-boundary dwell with no new machinery, whereas mine needed a knob plus a heuristic plus HUP-reinterpretation logic. Simpler wins.

One mechanical note for whenever kiosk mode gets built, since it constrains the implementation: "ignore HUPs" shouldn't be implemented as "auto-click Next at each boundary" or as "set dest to the finale" — the first gives zero dwell and the second triggers the rush path, which skips every beat. It wants to be a loop that plays chapters consecutively at authored pace, treating the HUP boundary as a no-op. Also, chapters that end in a riffle already carry that riffle's small trailing beat (300 or 100), so their kiosk dwell is the sum of that plus whatever you author — worth remembering when tuning.

Checking what npm audit reports in both projects.

Fixed — npm ci now reports 0 vulnerabilities. (npm audit classed them as 7 high, not critical, for what it's worth.)

All 7 were a single chain, and notably it lives in sqlite3's *build* toolchain, not in any code that runs in production: a DoS advisory in brace-expansion (GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg), reached via minimatch → glob → cacache → make-fetch-happen → node-gyp, which sqlite3 uses only to compile its native binding at install time. npm's suggested fix was npm audit fix --force, which would have installed sqlite3@6.0.1 — exactly the Render-breaking upgrade being avoided.

Instead, the fix reuses the mechanism already in place: package.json's overrides block was already forcing sqlite3's node-gyp to ^11.0.0 (evidently for an earlier round of the same problem). The 11.x line tops out at the still-vulnerable 11.5.0, so the override is now bumped to ^13.0.0, which pulls the fixed versions of the whole chain. sqlite3 itself stays at 5.1.7.

Two verifications after a full fresh npm ci: sqlite3's native binding loads, and the quals show the same 13 pre-existing CONSISTENT_AKRASIA_HORIZON failures as before — nothing new. jsbrain_server's audit was already clean.

One side effect worth knowing about: the allow-scripts guard had only puppeteer approved, so a fresh npm ci was silently skipping sqlite3's binding build and fsevents' install script — that would have eventually bitten as a "Could not locate the bindings file" crash. Both are now approved, which is why package.json's allowScripts block lists three entries in the diff.

what are these warnings about:

npm warn deprecated dottie@2.0.7: Package no longer supported. Contact Support at https://www.npmjs.com/support for more info.
npm warn deprecated prebuild-install@7.1.3: No longer maintained. Please contact the author of the relevant native addon; alternatives are available.
23:26 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 38s · 52s wall-clock time

Tracing where those two come from in the dependency tree.

Both are transitive and pinned in place by choices already made deliberately. Checking whether the newer versions of their parents would shed them.

Both are harmless deprecation notices about transitive dependencies, and neither is fixable from this repo — they're the registry authors flagging their own packages as unmaintained, which npm dutifully prints on every install. Neither is a vulnerability (the audit is clean); it's a different mechanism entirely.

dottie comes from sequelize (6.37.8, the latest stable). It's a tiny dot-notation helper sequelize uses to expand keys like "user.name" into nested objects when parsing query results. Its author deprecated the whole package, so every sequelize 6 install in the world prints this warning. The dependency only disappears in Sequelize 7, which is still in alpha (@sequelize/core 7.0.0-alpha.48) — not a sensible migration just to quiet a warning.

prebuild-install comes from sqlite3. It's the install-time tool that downloads sqlite3's prebuilt native binary (the alternative being a from-source node-gyp build). The prebuild team has stopped maintaining it in favor of newer tooling, but sqlite3 hasn't migrated — and notably, even the Render-blocked sqlite3@6.0.1 still depends on prebuild-install ^7.1.3, so this warning isn't even a casualty of the sqlite3 pin. It persists until the sqlite3 project switches tooling.

In both cases the code still works fine and only runs at install time (prebuild-install) or in a years-stable code path (dottie). Nothing actionable; the warnings will ride along until sequelize 7 goes stable and sqlite3 changes its binary-distribution tooling.

No change needed — the AGENTS.md rule is already enforced, twice over, just one level up: in the global [~/.claude/settings.json](/Users/dreeves/.claude/settings.json), which applies to this project (and every other one).

Two layers there:

  1. Deny rules: 31 explicit Bash(git <subcommand>:*) deny entries covering every mutating subcommand (add, commit, push, reset, rebase, stash, ...), with only git diff and git log on the allow list.
  2. A PreToolUse hook (~/.claude/hooks/git-guard.sh) on any git * command that works as an allowlist — only diff/log get through, so it catches anything the deny list might miss. This fired live earlier in this session: git show (not even a mutating command) got blocked by it.

Permission arrays *merge* across settings files rather than override, so the global deny list is fully in force here no matter what [.claude/settings.local.json](.claude/settings.local.json) says, and a local file can't un-deny a global deny. Adding the same list to settings.local.json would be pure duplication — two copies to keep in sync, protecting nothing extra. That confirms the parenthetical in AGENTS.md rule 14: it *is* enforced directly in settings.json, just the global one, which is the DRY location for a rule that's about the workflow in all repos rather than this repo specifically.

The only scenario where project-level rules would add anything: a session running where the global file doesn't exist — a cloud agent, another machine, a collaborator's checkout. settings.local.json wouldn't help there either, since it's untracked and never leaves this machine. The portable option would be a checked-in .claude/settings.json, but that imposes the git lockdown on everyone who uses Claude Code in the repo, including Uluc — say the word if that's wanted.

One housekeeping observation: .claude/settings.local.json is untracked but not listed in .gitignore, so it shows up as an untracked file for git. Standard practice is to gitignore it; happy to add that line.

Done — git show is now allowed alongside diff and log.

git show displays a git object: git show <sha> prints one commit's message plus its diff (roughly git log -1 -p for that commit), and git show <sha>:<path> prints a file's exact contents at a revision, which nothing in diff/log can do. It's strictly read-only — no way to touch the working tree, index, or refs — so it fits the spirit of the existing allowlist; it was only blocked because the guard enumerates allowed subcommands.

Three changes, all in the global config since that's where the policy lives:

  1. ~/.claude/hooks/git-guard.sh — the allowlist regex is now (diff|log|show), with the comment and denial message updated to match.
  2. ~/.claude/settings.json — added Bash(git show) and Bash(git show:*) allow rules so it runs without prompting.
  3. The git-command-permissions memory file and its index line now record diff/log/show, noting the addition was approved today.

Verified all three ways: the JSON parses, piping a synthetic git show payload through the hook passes while git push origin master still gets denied, and a live git show --stat HEAD ran without a prompt.
